metadata.summary: Use validated adult screening, quantify exposure, interpret alcohol biomarkers in context and assess fibrosis without treating an estimate as a diagnosis.
metadata.application: Turn the alcohol-use history, screening result, biomarker window and liver-stage evidence into a clear assessment and follow-up plan.
keyPoints: A positive brief screen needs a fuller assessment.
Count beverage volume and strength, not just containers.
A biomarker answers a time-limited exposure question.
Platelets and inflammation can confound fibrosis estimates.
Noninvasive staging and selective biopsy have different roles.

bodies.heading: Screen adults consistently and without assumptions
bodies.body: Use a validated brief alcohol-use screen in routine adult care rather than selecting patients by appearance or stereotypes. ACG recommends standardized, nonbiased screening across clinical settings. Ask about use with neutral language and an empathic, collaborative approach. The purpose is to identify unhealthy use and offer assessment and care, not to assign blame. Routine screening recommendations do not replace clinical evaluation when a person already has diagnosed AUD or is seeking treatment.

bodies.heading: Follow a positive screen with assessment
bodies.body: AUDIT-C has three questions about frequency, typical quantity and heavy-use occasions. The full AUDIT has ten questions and adds dependence-related features and alcohol-related problems. A positive brief screen prompts a more detailed risk assessment; it does not by itself diagnose AUD, cirrhosis or alcohol-associated hepatitis. Clarify the pattern, impaired control, consequences, last use and withdrawal history, then determine appropriate safety assessment, brief intervention or referral. Use the selected tool as validated rather than inventing a universal score cutoff.

bodies.heading: Count alcohol rather than containers
bodies.body: A U.S. standard drink contains about 14 g or 0.6 fluid ounces of pure alcohol. Examples are 12 fl oz of beer at 5% alcohol by volume (ABV), 5 fl oz of wine at 12% ABV, or 1.5 fl oz of spirits at 40% ABV. Serving sizes and strengths vary. For a beverage measured in fluid ounces, standard drinks = volume multiplied by ABV as a decimal, divided by 0.6. A 16 fl oz can at 7.5% ABV contains 16 times 0.075 = 1.2 fl oz of alcohol, or 2 standard drinks; two such cans contain 4. Record duration, frequency, heavy-use episodes and recent change as well as the total. A drink equivalent measures exposure, not a safe allowance for liver disease.

bodies.heading: Match the biomarker to the exposure window
bodies.body: Alcohol biomarkers supplement the interview and screening tools when they answer a clinical question. Select the specimen and test for the time period of interest. ACG Table 4 reports urine ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and ethyl sulfate (EtS) windows of 3-7 days and a blood phosphatidylethanol (PEth) window of about 30 days. These are reported detection windows, not guarantees for every patient or assay. Blood, urine and hair tests are not interchangeable. A negative short-window result cannot establish abstinence throughout an earlier month.

bodies.heading: Interpret an adjunct without overclaiming
bodies.body: Direct biomarkers such as EtG, EtS and PEth generally perform better for detecting exposure than indirect measures such as gamma-glutamyltransferase, mean corpuscular volume or carbohydrate-deficient transferrin. Indirect measures have substantial variability and limited utility. Neither a positive alcohol biomarker nor an isolated abnormal liver test determines AUD severity, exact alcohol quantity or fibrosis stage. ACG notes that biomarkers add no clinical utility simply to confirm heavy recent drinking already disclosed; they may help when a patient cannot be interviewed or the exposure history is uncertain. Interpret the result alongside the history, clinical findings and the assay limitations.

bodies.heading: Explain testing and protect access to care
bodies.body: Explain why a biomarker is being obtained, the time period it may reflect, its limitations and how the result will inform care. Use an ethical and transparent process. ACG specifically cautions that biomarker use in transplant assessment can have lasting stigmatizing effects and affect access to transplantation. A result should supplement assessment rather than substitute for a comprehensive psychosocial evaluation or become a judgment of character. Follow the clinical setting’s testing and consent process and use unexpected results to clarify the history and care needs.

bodies.heading: Assess fibrosis even before symptoms appear
bodies.body: People with suspected ALD may have fibrosis while feeling well. ACG identifies FIB-4, a blood-based score, and hepatic transient elastography as useful initial noninvasive fibrosis assessments. FIB-4 estimates risk from clinical laboratory information; transient elastography measures liver stiffness. Neither is an alcohol-use screen. Evaluate these results with other liver-stage evidence, competing causes of injury and the presence of complications. A reassuring aminotransferase value alone does not supply a complete fibrosis assessment.

bodies.heading: Recognize confounding before assigning a stage
bodies.body: Active alcohol use can lower platelet counts and affect the accuracy of FIB-4. Inflammation and steatohepatitis, particularly with markedly elevated AST or bilirubin, can overestimate liver stiffness on transient elastography. A high estimate during active injury should not automatically be called an exact irreversible fibrosis stage. Review the clinical setting and other stage evidence, and arrange further assessment when results are uncertain or discordant. Do not assume that every abnormal estimate is false or that a single improved laboratory value proves fibrosis has resolved.

bodies.heading: Resolve uncertainty and connect both kinds of care
bodies.body: Heavy alcohol use with noninvasive evidence of ALD warrants counseling about progression risk and referral to a clinician with liver expertise. Advanced fibrosis with ongoing drinking also needs addiction care. Liver biopsy is not routinely required just to stage ALD fibrosis; it may be appropriate when noninvasive assessment leaves diagnostic uncertainty or competing diagnoses. Maintain a plan for liver follow-up and sustained AUD care. Screening, a biomarker result or a fibrosis estimate is a starting point for a care pathway rather than the endpoint.

check.question: An adult has a positive AUDIT-C during routine screening. What is the best next step?
choices: Complete a nonjudgmental assessment of alcohol use, consequences and safety, then determine appropriate care.
Diagnose cirrhosis from the screening score.
Assign AUD severity from AUDIT-C alone without further assessment.
Order PEth to determine the exact fibrosis stage.
check.rationale: A positive brief screen calls for more detailed assessment to confirm unhealthy alcohol use and determine care. It does not establish a liver diagnosis or replace assessment of AUD features and safety.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-013.question: An adult screens positive on AUDIT-C at a routine visit. Which response best uses the result?
choices: Follow with a fuller alcohol-use and risk assessment to determine care.
Use the screen alone to diagnose alcohol-associated hepatitis.
Assign an exact fibrosis stage from the score.
Treat the result as a complete diagnostic assessment of AUD severity.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-013.rationale: USPSTF recommends follow-up assessment after a positive brief screen. Screening identifies a need for assessment; AUD severity and liver stage require additional evidence.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-014.question: Which distinction between AUDIT-C and the full AUDIT is correct?
choices: AUDIT-C has three consumption questions; the ten-item AUDIT also covers dependence-related features and problems.
AUDIT-C measures liver stiffness; the full AUDIT measures serum alcohol.
Both questionnaires have ten items with identical coverage.
The full AUDIT replaces all clinical assessment after a positive score.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-014.rationale: AUDIT-C asks about frequency, typical quantity and heavy-use occasions. The full AUDIT adds seven questions on dependence-related signs and alcohol-related problems; neither measures fibrosis or eliminates clinical assessment.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-015.question: A patient reports two 16 fl oz cans of beer at 7.5% ABV. Using 0.6 fl oz of alcohol per U.S. standard drink, how many standard drinks is this?
choices: 4 standard drinks.
2 standard drinks.
1.2 standard drinks.
8 standard drinks.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-015.rationale: Each can contains 16 × 0.075 = 1.2 fl oz of alcohol; 1.2 ÷ 0.6 = 2 standard drinks per can. Two cans contain 4 standard drinks. Container count alone understates exposure in this example.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-016.question: A clinic screens only adults whose appearance seems to suggest heavy alcohol use. Which change follows ACG guidance?
choices: Use standardized, nonbiased screening across clinical encounters rather than appearance-based selection.
Keep appearance-based selection and add a universal liver biopsy requirement.
Replace interview screening with an assumption based on occupation.
Screen only after a patient develops jaundice or ascites.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-016.rationale: ACG recommends standardized screening at medical encounters and attention to nonbiased practice. Clinical appearance or advanced symptoms should not be the gate for routine alcohol-use screening.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-017.question: Which exposure-window comparison matches ACG Table 4?
choices: Urine EtG/EtS reflect a shorter window of 3-7 days; blood PEth reflects about 30 days, with test limitations.
Urine EtG guarantees detection of every drinking episode during the previous year.
Blood PEth determines the exact hour of the last drink.
All alcohol biomarkers use the same specimen and detection window.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-017.rationale: ACG lists urine EtG and EtS windows of 3-7 days and blood PEth at 30 days. These are reported windows with variable performance, not guarantees of exact timing or identical detection.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-018.question: A negative urine EtG is obtained today. The clinical question concerns alcohol use three weeks earlier. What interpretation is justified?
choices: The negative short-window test cannot establish abstinence throughout that earlier period.
It proves there was no alcohol use in the entire preceding month.
It establishes that any liver injury has a nonalcohol cause.
It proves that AUD is absent regardless of the history.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-018.rationale: A urine EtG window of 3-7 days does not cover a use episode three weeks earlier. Select testing for the clinical time window and combine results with the history; a negative result does not independently exclude AUD or ALD.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-019.question: A positive PEth result is reviewed without any other assessment. Which conclusion goes beyond what the test establishes?
choices: It determines the patient’s exact fibrosis stage and AUD severity.
It provides exposure information to interpret with the clinical history.
It can supplement an alcohol-use assessment.
Its meaning depends on the assay and time window.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-019.rationale: PEth is an exposure biomarker, not a fibrosis-stage or AUD-severity test. The result should be interpreted with history, clinical assessment and its limitations.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-020.question: A patient clearly discloses heavy recent drinking. What does ACG say about obtaining a biomarker solely to confirm that disclosed exposure?
choices: It adds no clinical utility solely for that confirmation; testing should answer a specific clinical question.
It is required before any discussion of alcohol-related care.
It replaces assessment of withdrawal and liver disease.
It provides the exact amount consumed without an exposure history.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-020.rationale: ACG notes no added clinical utility from biomarkers in patients who disclose heavy recent drinking. Biomarkers may help when interview or exposure information is unavailable or uncertain; they do not replace other care or judge character.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-021.question: An asymptomatic patient has suspected ALD. Which pair does ACG identify as useful initial noninvasive fibrosis assessments?
choices: FIB-4 and hepatic transient elastography.
AUDIT-C and PEth as direct fibrosis-stage measurements.
Urine EtG and EtS as histologic fibrosis measurements.
Alcohol container count and an unstructured impression of liver symptoms.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-021.rationale: ACG identifies the blood-based FIB-4 score and transient elastography for initial noninvasive fibrosis assessment in ALD. Alcohol screening and exposure biomarkers answer different questions.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-022.question: FIB-4 is elevated during active alcohol use with a low platelet count. Which interpretation is strongest?
choices: Alcohol-related platelet reduction can affect the estimate; integrate other liver-stage evidence.
The score supplies an exact irreversible fibrosis stage regardless of the platelet change.
A low platelet count excludes advanced liver disease.
A positive AUDIT-C can be used to correct the FIB-4 numerically.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-022.rationale: ACG notes that active alcohol use may reduce platelets and affect FIB-4 accuracy. Context and other staging evidence are needed; neither declaring the estimate exact nor automatically excluding fibrosis is justified.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-023.question: Liver stiffness is high during marked inflammatory liver injury with elevated AST and bilirubin. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Inflammation can overestimate stiffness; interpret it with the clinical context and arrange further assessment if uncertain.
Stiffness always equals an exact fibrosis stage even during acute injury.
Elevated bilirubin proves the stiffness measurement is falsely low.
The result makes evaluation for competing liver disease unnecessary.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-023.rationale: ACG describes inflammation and steatohepatitis as confounders that can overestimate liver stiffness. Further contextual assessment is appropriate; the possibility of confounding neither proves nor excludes fibrosis.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-024.question: Noninvasive assessment leaves unresolved diagnostic uncertainty in suspected ALD. Which statement about biopsy is appropriate?
choices: Biopsy may help resolve uncertainty or competing diagnoses, although it is not routinely required just to stage fibrosis.
Every patient with harmful alcohol use must undergo biopsy before any counseling.
Biopsy can never be considered when noninvasive tests are inconclusive.
A urine alcohol biomarker provides the same diagnostic information as liver histology.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-024.rationale: ACG supports noninvasive staging and selective biopsy when diagnostic uncertainty remains. A biopsy requirement should not be applied universally, and exposure biomarkers do not supply liver histology.

wholeObject.question: FIB-4 is elevated during active alcohol use with a low platelet count. Which interpretation is strongest?
choices: Alcohol-related platelet reduction can affect the estimate; integrate other liver-stage evidence.
The score supplies an exact irreversible fibrosis stage regardless of the platelet change.
A low platelet count excludes advanced liver disease.
A positive AUDIT-C can be used to correct the FIB-4 numerically.

wholeObject.question: Liver stiffness is high during marked inflammatory liver injury with elevated AST and bilirubin. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Inflammation can overestimate stiffness; interpret it with the clinical context and arrange further assessment if uncertain.
Stiffness always equals an exact fibrosis stage even during acute injury.
Elevated bilirubin proves the stiffness measurement is falsely low.
The result makes evaluation for competing liver disease unnecessary.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG describes inflammation and steatohepatitis as confounders that can overestimate liver stiffness. Further contextual assessment is appropriate; the possibility of confounding neither proves nor excludes fibrosis.

wholeObject.question: Noninvasive assessment leaves unresolved diagnostic uncertainty in suspected ALD. Which statement about biopsy is appropriate?
choices: Biopsy may help resolve uncertainty or competing diagnoses, although it is not routinely required just to stage fibrosis.
Every patient with harmful alcohol use must undergo biopsy before any counseling.
Biopsy can never be considered when noninvasive tests are inconclusive.
A urine alcohol biomarker provides the same diagnostic information as liver histology.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG supports noninvasive staging and selective biopsy when diagnostic uncertainty remains. A biopsy requirement should not be applied universally, and exposure biomarkers do not supply liver histology.
